# Chapter 7 — OrgPath Across Three Surfaces — Resolving the Server Identity Problem

::: {.callout-note title="Requirement Being Addressed — Server Identity Coherence"}
The companion document required that organizational position be encoded consistently across all three representations of a server resource — the on-premises directory object, the cloud identity object, and the hybrid management plane resource record — using a common vocabulary derived from a single authoritative hierarchy registry, so that any tool reading any surface can determine the server's organizational position in the same terms.
:::

## The Three-Surface Problem and Its Resolution

A server operating in a hybrid environment simultaneously holds three identity representations. It is a computer object in the on-premises directory, with an organizational position defined by its OU placement. It is a device object in the cloud identity directory, registered through the hybrid identity join mechanism, with an organizational position that is not structurally defined by the cloud directory's flat object model. It is a managed resource in the hybrid management plane, with an organizational position loosely approximated by its resource group membership and resource tags — approximations that are not derived from any authoritative organizational registry and that are not expressed in any vocabulary compatible with the OrgPath values stamped on user and device identities. These three representations exist independently. No native platform mechanism links them. The companion document identified this fragmentation as one of the most practically consequential gaps in the hybrid governance model: a server that exists on three surfaces in three independent representations cannot be queried, governed, or decommissioned coherently using the native tools of any of those surfaces.

When a server is onboarded to the hybrid management plane — whether it is being migrated from an existing on-premises deployment or being provisioned for the first time — the governance pipeline performs three operations in sequence. It determines the server's organizational assignment from the OrgTree registry, using the server's existing OU placement as the source of truth if the server is an existing system being brought under management, or from the provisioning record if the server is being built fresh. It derives the OrgPath value for that assignment. It stamps that value on all three representations of the server: as an extended attribute on the on-premises computer object, as an extended attribute on the cloud device identity, and as a resource tag on the hybrid management plane resource record. From the moment of onboarding, the server carries the same OrgPath value on all three surfaces, expressed in the same format, derived from the same registry.

## The Governance Consequence of Uniformity

The governance consequence of this uniformity is substantial. Any tool that can read any one of the three surfaces can now determine the server's organizational position and express it in terms that are directly comparable to the organizational position of any user or device. A query for all assets belonging to a given division returns users, devices, and servers together — because all of them carry OrgPath values derived from the same OrgTree, formatted identically, and stored on their respective management surfaces under the same attribute name or tag key. Incident response operations that require enumerating all assets belonging to a compromised organizational unit return a complete picture across all asset types. Compliance reporting that requires demonstrating that all assets in a given segment of the organization are governed under a specific policy framework can be produced from a single query against a single attribute. Dependency analysis that requires identifying all server assets in a given division before a decommissioning event can be executed without manual cross-referencing of three independent inventories.

## Detecting and Correcting Representation Divergence

The three representations of a server are no longer independent identity objects that happen to reference the same hardware. They are views of a single governed asset, unified by the OrgPath value they share. If the OrgPath values across the three representations diverge — because one surface was updated by an out-of-band administrative action and the others were not updated to match, or because a migration event updated the on-premises representation but the pipeline failed to propagate the change to the cloud and management plane representations — the drift detection mechanism identifies the divergence. The drift detection process reads the OrgPath value from each of the three surfaces for every server in scope and compares them. A divergence between surfaces is reported as a cross-surface inconsistency finding, classified at high severity, and the pipeline reconciles the representations by reapplying the authoritative value from the OrgTree registry to all three surfaces in a single pipeline run. The authoritative value is always the one derived from the OrgTree registry — not the value on any particular surface, which may have been set by an out-of-band operation and may not reflect the governed organizational assignment.
